summary: This clipped NASA Vital Signs page explains atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) as a heat-trapping greenhouse gas, emitted by fossil fuel burning, wildfires and volcanoes. It reports that human activities raised atmospheric CO2 by 50% since 1750, to 150% of its 1750 value, and that the Mauna Loa record and ice-core records show this rise. It also describes the seasonal sawtooth cycle driven by Northern and Southern Hemisphere plant growth and decomposition, with the long-term upward trend caused mainly by fossil fuel emissions.
one_line: NASA Vital Signs page on atmospheric carbon dioxide: its greenhouse warming, the human-driven 50% rise since 1750, and its seasonal cycle.
key_facts: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is an important heat-trapping gas, also known as a greenhouse gas.
Latest measurement of atmospheric CO2 on the page is 425 ppm, for February 2024.
Human activities have raised the atmosphere's carbon dioxide content by 50% in less than 200 years.
Since the onset of industrial times in the 18th century, human activities have raised atmospheric CO2 by 50%, meaning CO2 is now 150% of its value in 1750.
The human-induced rise in CO2 is greater than the natural increase observed at the end of the last ice age 20,000 years ago.
The first graph shows atmospheric CO2 levels measured by NOAA at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, since 1958.
The second graph shows CO2 levels during Earth's last three glacial cycles, captured by air bubbles trapped in ice sheets and glaciers.
The animated map shows CO2 rising from 365 parts per million (ppm) in 2002 to over 420 ppm currently.
Parts per million refers to the number of carbon dioxide molecules per million molecules of dry air.
The mid-troposphere measurements are taken from the layer 8 to 12 kilometers (about 5 to 7 miles) above the ground.
The annual rise and fall of CO2 is caused by seasonal cycles in photosynthesis on a massive scale.
In Northern Hemisphere spring, plants draw in CO2 to fuel growth, and in northern autumn plant matter decomposes and releases CO2 back to the atmosphere.
Because there is much more land and vegetation in the Northern Hemisphere, the global seasonal cycle more closely aligns with the northern pattern.
The upward climb of the CO2 trend line over decades is caused by CO2 emissions, primarily from burning fossil fuels.
